paragraphs.heading: Two stars, one orbit
paragraphs.text: A binary star is a pair of stars held together by their gravity and circling each other. Today the name is usually kept for pairs that revolve around a shared center of mass. The looser term double star covers any two stars that simply look close together in the sky. Some doubles are true binaries, but others are optical doubles: two stars at very different distances from the Sun that only happen to line up.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Binaries are among the most important objects in astrophysics. Studying them lets astronomers measure the masses of stars directly and put theories of how stars evolve to the test. When the two stars sit close together, their gravity can pull each other's outer atmospheres out of shape. Some close pairs even trade mass, which can carry them into stages a lone star never reaches. Binaries also sit at the heart of many planetary nebulae, and they give rise to novae and type Ia supernovae.

paragraphs.heading: Four ways to spot one
paragraphs.text: Astronomers sort binaries by how they are detected. A visual binary is one that a telescope can split into two separate stars. A spectroscopic binary reveals itself through periodic changes in its spectral lines. A photometric binary dims when one star eclipses the other, and an astrometric binary shows up when a star's position strays because of a companion nobody can see. A single pair can belong to more than one of these groups.

paragraphs.heading: Mapping an orbit
paragraphs.text: In a visual binary, the brighter star is called the primary and the dimmer one the secondary. Each time they look, observers note the direction and the angular gap from the primary to the secondary, along with the time. After enough of these records, they plot the points around the primary and fit the most likely ellipse that obeys Kepler's law of areas. That shape, the apparent ellipse, is the real orbit projected onto the plane of the sky.

paragraphs.heading: Early discoveries
paragraphs.text: Pairs of stars that look close together have been seen ever since the telescope was invented; Riccioli saw Mizar in the Big Dipper as double in 1650. In 1767 John Michell used statistics to show that stars come in pairs and groups far more often than chance alignment could explain, and he suggested gravity might draw them together. William Herschel began watching double stars in 1779, hoping to use them to measure the distance to nearby stars. By 1803 he had seen many pairs shift over 25 years in a way that looked like orbiting rather than parallax.

paragraphs.heading: Famous pairs and big catalogs
paragraphs.text: Sirius is a binary, and so is Cygnus X-1, a well-known black hole. The first binary orbit ever worked out was that of Xi Ursae Majoris, computed by Félix Savary in 1827. As of June 2017 the Washington Double Star Catalog listed more than 100,000 double stars, yet orbits are known for only a few thousand. Many visual binaries need centuries or millennia to go around once, and for most of them only part of a circuit has been seen.
